partycohesion:
Do members of Congress vote the same way no matter who is president? PartyCohesion shows how often each member votes with their own party, using every House and Senate roll call since 2007 from the official record.

Data: Voteview
https://rendellrich.github.io/partycohesion/
same-bill-different-vote:
Most bills get more than one floor vote. Since 2007, members of Congress voted for a bill at one stage and against it at another 3,718 times while most of their own party voted the same way both times. Bills often change between votes, so a different vote is not a contradiction.

Data: Voteview
https://rendellrich.github.io/partycohesion/same-bill-different-vote/
respect-for-marriage-act:
The Respect for Marriage Act had two House votes in 2022. In July, 47 House Republicans voted Yea. In December, after the Senate added religious-liberty language, 39 did. Of the Republicans who voted both times, 9 voted differently the second time.

Data: Voteview, House roll calls 373 and 513
https://rendellrich.github.io/partycohesion/respect-for-marriage-act/
senate-unity:
How often do senators vote with their own party? At each of the last three changes of president (2017, 2021, 2025), senators from the new president's party voted with their party more often than in the Congress before, and the other party's senators less often. In the current Congress, still in session: Senate Republicans 98.6%, Senate Democrats 95.3%.

Data: Voteview
https://rendellrich.github.io/partycohesion/senate-unity/
floor-remarks:
Members who took a clear position in floor debate on Ukraine aid (2023 to 2024) or the Respect for Marriage Act (2022), and how they voted on the final bill: 101 of 101 House members and 44 of 47 senators voted the way they spoke.

Data: Congressional Record (GovInfo), Voteview
https://rendellrich.github.io/partycohesion/floor-remarks/
congress-final:
The 118th Congress (2023 to 2024) is complete. Its final party unity record, the average share of party-line votes on which members sided with their own party: House Democrats 96.7%, House Republicans 93.0%, Senate Democrats 98.3%, Senate Republicans 90.5%. That's over 871 House and 538 Senate party-line votes, where most Democrats and most Republicans voted on opposite sides.

Data: Voteview
https://rendellrich.github.io/partycohesion/congress-final/
